Fenced
fĕnst
adj. and v. (walled, defended, hedged about — in the KJV the standing word for a fortified city, for a planted vineyard, and for the frame of a man's body)
From Middle English fensen, a shortening of defensen, to defend; so a fence is a defence before it is a boundary. The KJV uses it to render several Hebrew words for walling, hedging, and cutting off.

Biblical Definition

Fenced in the Authorized Version means fortified, and it is used in three registers that repay attention. Militarily it describes the walled towns of Canaan and Judah: “All these cities were fenced with high walls, gates, and bars; beside unwalled towns a great many” (Deu 3:5), and the terrible sentence of Hezekiah's fourteenth year, when Sennacherib “come up against all the fenced cities of Judah, and took them” (2Ki 18:13) — every fortification in the kingdom fell, and Jerusalem was spared not by its walls but by an angel. Agriculturally it describes God's labour on His vineyard: “he fenced it, and gathered out the stones thereof, and planted it with the choicest vine” (Isa 5:2), and the whole tragedy of that song is that the vineyard, given everything, brought forth wild grapes — whereupon the LORD says He will take away the hedge and break down the wall. And anatomically, in the most surprising use of all, Job says of his own frame: “Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh, and hast fenced me with bones and sinews” (Job 10:11). The body is a walled city. In every register the point is the same: what is fenced is fenced by another, and stands only while He maintains the wall.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines fenced as enclosed with a fence, guarded, fortified; and fence as a wall, hedge or enclosure raised to defend, from the verb to fend or defend.

expand to see more

FENCED, pp. Enclosed with a fence; guarded; fortified.

FENCE, n. That which defends; a wall, hedge, ditch, bank, or line of posts and rails, raised for the security of enclosed ground.

A fenced city, in Scripture, is a city surrounded with a wall, in distinction from an unwalled town or village.

The word is a contraction of defence, from the verb to fend, to keep off.

FENCE, v.t. To enclose with a hedge, wall or other barrier; to guard; to fortify.

Key Scripture

Deu 3:5 — "All these cities were fenced with high walls, gates, and bars; beside unwalled towns a great many."

2Ki 18:13 — "Now in the fourteenth year of king Hezekiah did Sennacherib king of Assyria come up against all the fenced cities of Judah, and took them."

Isa 5:2 — "And he fenced it, and gathered out the stones thereof, and planted it with the choicest vine, and built a tower in the midst of it, and also made a winepress therein: and he looked that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes."

Job 10:11 — "Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh, and hast fenced me with bones and sinews."

Modern Corruption

Security is sought in the fence — the wall, the policy, the reserve fund — when Scripture makes the fence itself a gift held at God's pleasure, removable in a single season.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what Scripture consistently does with fortifications. Judah had a whole system of fenced cities, and in one campaign Sennacherib took every one of them. Isaiah's vineyard had a hedge and a wall, and the judgment announced is simply their removal: “I will take away the hedge thereof, and it shall be eaten up; and break down the wall thereof, and it shall be trodden down” (Isa 5:5). The Bible is not against walls — Nehemiah built one and it was a work of God — but it will not let a man rest in one. “Except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain” (Psa 127:1).

Job 10:11 is the sentence to carry away. A man's own body is described as a fortification God built — skin and flesh for the covering, bones and sinews for the wall — and Job says it in the middle of an argument about why God is now pulling it down. The doctrine of creation reaches all the way into the frame: “I am fearfully and wonderfully made” (Psa 139:14), which forbids both the contempt for the body that gnosticism teaches and the worship of it that the present age teaches. And the same hand that fenced it will one day take the fence down, and raise it again incorruptible.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

English fence, from defence; rendering Hebrew batsar (H1219), to cut off, make inaccessible, fortify; suk (H7753), to hedge about; 'azaq (H5823), to dig about.

expand to see more

Hebrew batsar (H1219) — to cut off, enclose, fortify; the word behind “fenced cities”.

Hebrew mibtsar (H4013) — a fortress, stronghold; the noun from the same root.

Hebrew suk (H7753) — to hedge, fence about; used of the hedge Satan complains God set around Job (Job 1:10).

Hebrew 'azaq (H5823) — to dig about, fence in; the verb of Isa 5:2.

Hebrew sakak (H5526) — to cover, screen, hedge in; used of God covering David in the day of battle (Psa 140:7).

Usage

"“Fenced with high walls, gates, and bars” — the cities of the land."

"“He fenced it, and gathered out the stones thereof” — God's labour on His vineyard."

"“Hast fenced me with bones and sinews” — the body as a walled city."
